foods.benefits_en: Watermelon is roughly 92% water with a useful electrolyte profile (potassium, magnesium) and a distinctive carotenoid — **lycopene** — at concentrations rivalling cooked tomato. It also carries **citrulline**, an amino acid associated with vascular and exercise-recovery markers in small trials. Neither Blueprint nor Longo names it explicitly, but it sits comfortably in both patterns as a summer hydration and fruit slot.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Eat fresh, ideally chilled, in generous wedges during hot weather. The flesh closest to the rind carries more citrulline; the deep red centre is more lycopene-dense. Frozen cubes work in smoothies. Pair with feta and mint for a classic Mediterranean salad.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Seasonal — summer. A daily fruit slot during the season; the high water content makes it a useful hot-weather food.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category specific to watermelon. The broader lycopene/carotenoid gap noted for tomato applies — diets chronically low in red/orange produce miss out on the carotenoid family.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake. Very large single servings can act as a mild diuretic given the water and potassium load.

foods.benefits_en: Raisins are dried grapes — they concentrate the potassium, iron, boron, and polyphenols of the fresh fruit as water leaves. They're a useful traditional iron source in plant-leaning diets and a quick-energy food for endurance work. Longo's pattern includes them sparingly, typically as a sweet accent in grain dishes or as the paired sweet with nuts.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Small handfuls, ideally paired with nuts to blunt the sugar curve. Add to oats, grain salads, tagines, or baked goods. Soak briefly in warm water, wine, or rum if they've dried out hard. Look for unsulfured varieties when possible — the brown ones rather than the pale golden ones.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Sparingly. A small daily handful is fine in Longo's pattern, inside the eating window. The fresh grape is a different proposition — eat that more freely in season.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category specific to raisins.
foods.excess_signs_en: The concentrated sugar load is the main concern — habitual large handfuls push glycemic load and stick to teeth, contributing to dental wear. Small daily portions sit comfortably; bowl-a-day intake does not.

foods.benefits_en: Fresh cranberries carry **proanthocyanidins** — a polyphenol family particularly studied for urinary-tract markers — alongside vitamin C and fibre. The dried form concentrates these compounds but also concentrates sugar, and most commercial dried cranberries are sweetened heavily because the raw fruit is too tart to eat unsweetened. Read the label: cranberries sweetened with apple juice or used unsweetened are the version to look for.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Small portions, scattered into grain salads, oats, yoghurt, or baked goods. Pair with nuts to blunt the sugar curve. The unsweetened or apple-juice-sweetened versions are nutritionally cleaner; the standard sugar-sweetened "craisins" are closer to candy. Fresh or frozen cranberries are a different and more polyphenol-dense proposition when you can find them.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Sparingly, as a flavour accent rather than a daily fruit slot.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category specific to cranberries.
foods.excess_signs_en: The concentrated sugar load (especially in sweetened versions) is the main concern. Habitual large handfuls push glycemic load. No commonly-reported systemic excess pattern at culinary intake of the unsweetened form.

foods.benefits_en: A blend of blueberries, strawberries, blackberries, raspberries, and (sometimes) blackcurrants carries the full anthocyanin / ellagitannin / vitamin-C spread of the berry family in one handful. The rotation is the point: different pigments map to different polyphenol classes, and eating across the range covers more of the family than any single berry does. Blueprint leans on blueberries specifically, but a mixed-berry blend is the broader Longo-compatible move.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Fresh in season; frozen out of season — the freezing process barely touches the polyphenol or vitamin content, and frozen mixed berries are usually cheaper and more polyphenol-dense than off-season fresh ones. Stir into yoghurt, oats, or salads; blend into smoothies; warm gently as a compote for pancakes. Pair with nuts or fat for slower sugar release.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily. A cup of mixed berries a day is a reasonable default across both reference patterns.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category. The broader anthocyanin/polyphenol gap from diets chronically devoid of dark fruit tracks in cohort data with worse cognitive-aging markers.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: Basil is the aromatic backbone of Mediterranean cooking — its essential-oil profile (eugenol, linalool, methyl chavicol) carries antimicrobial and anti-inflammatory activity in lab studies, and the leaves bring a small but real load of vitamin K and beta-carotene. Longo's recipes lean heavily on basil — pesto, tomato-basil pastas, finishing leaves on caprese-style dishes. Blueprint uses it less but accepts it freely. It's a culinary herb, not a daily required food, but the flavour payoff makes it one of the easier ways to keep fresh greens in the diet.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Add at the end of cooking — basil's aromatics are volatile and the leaves blacken with sustained heat. Tear rather than chop with a steel blade if you want the brightest flavour (the metal accelerates oxidation). Classic preparations: pesto (raw, blended with pine nuts, garlic, olive oil, Parmesan), torn over tomato salads, finishing over soup. Store the stems in water like cut flowers, not in the fridge — basil blackens at low temperatures.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily in summer when the plant is in season; otherwise as available. No specific timing.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category — basil is a culinary herb, not an essential nutrient.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: Parsley is more nutritionally substantial than it looks — by weight it's a vitamin-K, vitamin-C, and folate concentrate, plus a flavonoid (apigenin, luteolin) source and an apiol/myristicin aromatic load. Italian flat-leaf parsley is the cooking variety; curly parsley is largely garnish. Longo's recipes use parsley generously — gremolata, tabbouleh-style salads, finishing on fish and beans. Treat it as a leafy green you happen to call an herb, not a sprig of garnish.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Use the leaves in volume — a quarter-cup chopped flat-leaf parsley folded into a grain salad, a small bowl as the bulk of tabbouleh, a handful in gremolata. The stems are edible and carry most of the same compounds; chop them finely and use. Add at the end of cooking to keep the vitamin C intact. Pairs with lemon zest and garlic (the gremolata triplet).
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily is reasonable when in season. No specific timing.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category specific to parsley, but diets chronically low in dark leafy greens track in cohort data with worse vitamin-K and folate markers.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake. Concentrated parsley-seed oil is a different and traditionally medicinal preparation — not relevant at kitchen doses of the leaf.

foods.benefits_en: Cilantro (the leaf; coriander is the seed) carries a distinctive aromatic-aldehyde profile that splits opinion sharply — a subset of people with a variant of the **OR6A2** olfactory receptor gene perceive it as soapy rather than herbal. For those who can stand it, the leaves bring vitamin K, vitamin C, and a polyphenol set (quercetin, kaempferol) plus some lab-study interest in heavy-metal chelation. It's the signature herb of Latin American and South Asian cooking and a useful rotation partner to parsley.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Add at the end of cooking — the aromatics are volatile. Stems are edible and often more flavour-dense than leaves; chop and use. Classic pairings: lime + chili (the cilantro triplet), folded into bean dishes, scattered over fish tacos or curries. If you're cooking for someone with the OR6A2 variant, parsley or basil substitute reasonably.
foods.when_to_consume_en: As available — no specific timing.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category — cilantro is a culinary herb, not an essential nutrient.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: Mint's signature compound is **menthol**, which carries mild antimicrobial and digestive-soothing activity — the traditional after-meal mint tea of North Africa and the Middle East has a real basis in motility and gas relief. The leaves also deliver small amounts of vitamin A, vitamin C, and rosmarinic acid. Longo's Mediterranean roots use mint across yoghurt sauces, grain salads (tabbouleh), and infusions; Blueprint uses it less but accepts it freely.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Tear or chop at the end of cooking — menthol is volatile and bruising releases more of it than clean knife cuts. Classic preparations: mint tea (fresh leaves steeped in hot water), tabbouleh (mint + parsley + bulgur + lemon), yoghurt sauces (tzatziki-style), pea-and-mint soups. Pair with lamb, peas, cucumber, watermelon, dark chocolate.
foods.when_to_consume_en: After meals as tea is a traditional and reasonable habit, particularly for people prone to bloating. Otherwise as available.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category — mint is a culinary herb, not an essential nutrient.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake. Concentrated peppermint oil is a different preparation and can lower lower-esophageal sphincter tone — relevant for reflux at therapeutic doses, not at culinary ones.

foods.benefits_en: Rosemary carries **carnosic acid**, **carnosol**, and **rosmarinic acid** — a polyphenol/diterpene set studied for cognitive and anti-inflammatory markers. The aromatic oils (cineole, camphor, pinene) make rosemary one of the few herbs that genuinely strengthens with heat, which is why it's a roasting and grilling staple. Longo's Tuscan-leaning recipes use rosemary across roasted vegetables, beans, and focaccia; Blueprint uses it less frequently.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Sprigs go in early with roasting vegetables, beans, or potatoes — heat coaxes the oils out rather than destroying them. Strip the needles from the stem and chop finely if you want them dispersed in the dish; whole sprigs are fished out before serving. Pair with olive oil, garlic, lemon, white beans. A small sprig is usually enough — the flavour is assertive.
foods.when_to_consume_en: As available — no specific timing.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category — rosemary is a culinary herb, not an essential nutrient.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: Sage carries **thujone**, **camphor**, and **rosmarinic acid** — a polyphenol/terpene profile with the strongest cognitive-marker literature among the common kitchen herbs (small trials note effects on memory tasks at culinary-adjacent doses). The flavour is assertive and slightly bitter; a little goes a long way. Longo's Tuscan corpus uses sage with white beans, pumpkin, and brown butter; Blueprint uses it sparingly.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Tear or chop fresh leaves at the end of cooking, or fry whole leaves briefly in olive oil or butter for a crispy garnish (a classic over pumpkin gnocchi or white beans). Dry sage is stronger per gram than fresh and works well in stuffings and rubs. Pair with white beans, winter squash, pork, brown butter, lemon.
foods.when_to_consume_en: As available — no specific timing.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category — sage is a culinary herb, not an essential nutrient.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake. Concentrated sage essential oil and prolonged high-dose sage-tea regimens carry thujone-load concerns at therapeutic-dose levels — not relevant at kitchen doses of the leaf.

foods.benefits_en: "Mixed herbs" in the Mediterranean kitchen usually means a dried blend of **oregano, thyme, basil, and rosemary** — the Italian seasoning / herbes de Provence pattern. Each contributes its own essential-oil profile (carvacrol from oregano, thymol from thyme, eugenol from basil, carnosic acid from rosemary), and the blend as a whole carries one of the highest antioxidant densities of any dried-pantry item per gram. Longo's pasta sauces, bean stews, and roasted vegetables lean on this blend reflexively; Blueprint uses Italian seasoning across many of its savoury recipes.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Dried blends are added early — they need heat and time to bloom, and they tolerate sustained cooking far better than the fresh equivalents. Stir into soffrito with the onions, into tomato sauce as it reduces, or onto vegetables before roasting. A teaspoon goes a long way. Store in a dark jar; dried herbs lose potency after about a year on the shelf — replace annually for the cleanest flavour.
foods.when_to_consume_en: As available — no specific timing.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category — mixed herbs are culinary, not an essential nutrient.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: The chickpea is the workhorse of both reference patterns. Longo treats it as one of the cornerstone legumes of the longevity diet — high plant-protein, high fibre, low glycemic load, with a folate, iron, and manganese profile that anchors the Mediterranean-pescatarian frame. Blueprint relies on chickpea flour for the **nutty-flour bowl** that's a recurring breakfast / lunch base in the protocol, and on whole chickpeas for stews and salads. Both corpuses lean on it heavily.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Dried chickpeas, soaked overnight and simmered, hold the firmest texture and the cleanest flavour; canned chickpeas (rinsed) are a faster default and nutritionally close. Pair with olive oil, lemon, tahini, cumin, parsley (the hummus axis) or with tomato and rosemary (the Tuscan stew axis). Chickpea flour (farinata, socca, the Blueprint nutty-flour bowl) is a useful gluten-free flour with the same protein and fibre profile. Roasted chickpeas make a crunchy snack with a protein-fat profile better than most savoury snacks.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily is fine in Longo's pattern. A cup of cooked chickpeas a day is well inside the longevity-diet frame. Inside the eating window; no specific timing.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a chickpea-specific deficiency, but diets chronically low in legumes broadly track in cohort data with worse fibre, folate, and plant-protein markers — and with the cardiovascular and metabolic patterns those gaps imply.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake. Sudden large increases in legume intake can produce transient bloating as the gut microbiome adapts — ramp up gradually if you're new to them.

foods.benefits_en: Lentils are the fastest-cooking common legume and one of the most plant-protein- and iron-dense — green, brown, black (beluga), and red varieties each carry slightly different textures but a similar nutritional core. They're a Longo staple — the Italian lentil-and-rice (riso e lenticchie) and lentil soup traditions sit squarely inside the longevity diet. Lentils also carry a useful polyphenol load in the seed coat (more in the dark varieties).
foods.how_to_consume_en: No soak required — rinse and simmer. Green and brown lentils hold their shape (good for salads and stews); red lentils dissolve into a creamy texture (good for dal and soup); black beluga lentils hold their shape and look striking on the plate. Pair with cumin, coriander, garlic, lemon, and olive oil; squeeze lemon at the table to help non-heme iron absorption.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily is fine. A bowl of lentil soup or stew sits comfortably inside both reference patterns. Inside the eating window; no specific timing.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a lentil-specific deficiency. The broader pattern noted for chickpeas — diets chronically low in legumes track with worse fibre, folate, and plant-protein markers — applies.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake. Same gut-adaptation note as chickpeas — ramp up gradually if legumes are new.

foods.benefits_en: Black beans carry the standard legume profile (plant protein, fibre, folate, iron) plus an anthocyanin load in the dark seed coat that puts them at the polyphenol-dense end of the bean family. They're the staple bean of Latin American kitchens — black beans and rice (a complete-protein pairing) is one of the more nutritionally complete one-pot foods in common rotation. Longo accepts black beans within the broader legume slot; Blueprint uses them less frequently than chickpeas.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Dried beans, soaked overnight and simmered with bay and garlic, hold the cleanest flavour and texture; canned (rinsed) is the faster default. Pair with cumin, oregano, lime, cilantro, chili (the Latin American axis) or with rice for the classic complete-protein pairing. Black-bean soup, refried black beans, and black-bean salads all keep the seed-coat polyphenols on the plate.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily is fine within the broader legume rotation. Inside the eating window; no specific timing.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a black-bean-specific deficiency. The broader low-legume pattern applies.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake. Same gut-adaptation note as the other legumes.

foods.benefits_en: "Mixed dried beans" in Longo's corpus usually means the Italian white-and-pink axis — **cannellini** (white kidney), **borlotti** (cranberry bean), and sometimes **lamon** beans — that anchors Tuscan and northern-Italian bean cookery. The nutritional core is the standard legume profile (plant protein, fibre, folate, iron, manganese) with subtle texture and flavour differences across varieties. The point of cooking them mixed is the slow, layered texture of a bean stew that no single variety achieves alone.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Soak overnight, then simmer slowly with bay, sage, garlic, and olive oil — the Tuscan way is to cook them gently for hours until the skins are soft but intact. Pair with rosemary, sage, tomato, kale, farro. Pasta e fagioli (pasta and beans) is the canonical use; ribollita and minestrone fold them into vegetable stews. Save the cooking liquid — it carries flavour and starch that thickens whatever you're making.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily is fine within Longo's pattern. Inside the eating window; no specific timing. The classic Italian context is lunch or early evening, with bread and olive oil.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category specific to mixed beans. The broader low-legume pattern applies — diets chronically low in legumes track with worse fibre, folate, and plant-protein markers.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake. Same gut-adaptation note as the other legumes — ramp up gradually if they're new to the diet.

foods.benefits_en: Chestnuts are the outlier of the nut family — low in fat, high in slow-burning starch, and the only common nut that behaves nutritionally more like a grain. Dried chestnuts concentrate that starch alongside potassium, magnesium, manganese, and a modest fibre payload. They are naturally gluten-free, which is why mountain cuisines from the Apennines to Corsica leaned on them for centuries as a staple flour and pot food. Longo's tradition reaches for chestnuts as a Mediterranean autumn carbohydrate; Blueprint doesn't feature them explicitly, but they fit the whole-food, low-glycemic-index pattern.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Soak dried chestnuts overnight, then simmer 45–60 minutes until tender — they finish softer and sweeter than canned. Use them whole in stews and soups (the classic pairing is with cavolo nero, borlotti beans, and a parmesan rind), pureed into autumn vegetable soups, or ground into flour for flatbreads and pancakes. Their sweetness pairs well with bay leaf, rosemary, and a finishing drizzle of EVOO. Don't skip the soak; dried chestnuts cooked from hard are mealy.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Seasonal — autumn and winter, when their warming starch fits the pattern. Inside Longo's 12h eating window like any other carbohydrate. A 50–80 g cooked portion sits comfortably alongside legumes and greens as a complete plate.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category on its own. Diets chronically low in whole-food complex carbohydrates — chestnuts, intact grains, tubers — often track with low energy on long days and the blood-sugar swings that come from leaning on refined starches instead.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake. Like any starchy food, very large portions can push past energy balance if they replace rather than complement vegetables and legumes.

foods.benefits_en: Spelt is an ancient relative of modern wheat that kept a tougher hull and a less-bred genome through the centuries. Compared to common wheat it carries slightly more protein, more zinc and magnesium, and a fibre profile that tends to feel gentler on the gut — though it still contains gluten and is not safe for coeliacs. Whole-grain spelt (farro) is the form Longo's tradition treats as a Mediterranean longevity grain, eaten in soups, salads, and pilafs across central Italy. Blueprint uses whole grains in the same spirit but doesn't single spelt out.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Cook whole spelt berries (farro) like rice — 25–35 minutes simmered in salted water until chewy but tender; pearled spelt is faster. Use cold in grain salads with chickpeas, parsley, lemon, and EVOO, or hot in the Tuscan **zuppa di farro** with borlotti beans and cavolo nero. Spelt flour bakes into denser, nuttier loaves than 00 wheat flour and works well at a 30–50% blend with wheat for sourdough.
foods.when_to_consume_en: A regular grain rotation alongside brown rice, barley, and oats hits the whole-grain target both reference patterns push. Inside Longo's 12h eating window, paired with legumes and a vegetable.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: No spelt-specific deficiency. Diets chronically low in whole, intact grains tend to track with lower fibre, lower magnesium, and the gut-microbiome thinning that comes with a refined-carb pattern.
foods.excess_signs_en: Spelt contains gluten — people with coeliac disease or non-coeliac gluten sensitivity will react to it. Beyond that, no commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: Brown rice keeps the bran and germ that white milling strips away, which is where most of the fibre, magnesium, manganese, and B-vitamin payload lives. The glycemic load is meaningfully lower than white rice for the same cooked weight, and the fibre slows the glucose curve enough that brown rice fits a longevity carbohydrate pattern where white rice doesn't quite. Both Blueprint and Longo treat whole grains as the default; semi-brown (partially milled) is a reasonable middle ground when full brown rice feels too dense.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Rinse, then simmer 35–45 minutes in roughly 2:1 water to rice until tender — much longer than white rice, and worth the wait. A pinch of salt and a bay leaf in the water lifts the flavour. Pairs naturally with legumes (the rice-and-beans combination delivers a complete amino-acid profile), roasted vegetables, and a finishing splash of tamari or EVOO. Batch-cook and refrigerate; cooled and reheated rice carries more resistant starch, which feeds gut bacteria.
foods.when_to_consume_en: A staple carbohydrate, eaten in the eating window. Roughly 60–80 g dry per portion is a comfortable plate size. Both reference patterns rotate it freely across the week.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: No rice-specific deficiency. Diets chronically low in whole grains track with lower fibre intake and the slower gut transit that often comes with that pattern.
foods.excess_signs_en: Brown rice — and rice broadly — accumulates arsenic from the soil more than most grains. The cohort signal is small at normal intakes; rinsing thoroughly and cooking in excess water (then draining) reduces it further. Rotating rice with spelt, barley, oats, and quinoa avoids leaning on any one grain.

foods.benefits_en: Pasta made from durum-wheat semolina has a denser protein matrix than soft-wheat noodles, which slows starch release and gives it a lower glycemic load than bread of equivalent weight — especially when cooked **al dente**. That structural quirk is part of why the Mediterranean pattern can lean on pasta several times a week without the metabolic cost a refined-starch diet would carry. Longo treats pasta as a central plate of the longevity diet; Blueprint doesn't feature pasta directly but tolerates it inside a whole-grain frame.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Cook **al dente** — firm to the bite — in heavily salted water, then finish in the sauce rather than dressing it on the plate. Pair with legumes (pasta e ceci, pasta e fagioli), vegetables (pasta with broccoli, with cavolo nero, with tomato and basil), and EVOO; the longevity move is to treat pasta as the carbohydrate scaffold for a bean-and-vegetable plate, not as a standalone dish. Whole-wheat pasta swaps in some bran and germ at the cost of texture; it's a reasonable rotation.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Inside the eating window. Longo's tradition puts pasta at lunch more often than dinner — daytime carbohydrate sits more comfortably with circadian metabolism. A 70–80 g dry portion is the Mediterranean default.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category. Diets that strip carbohydrates entirely often track with low energy and disrupted sleep over the long term.
foods.excess_signs_en: Pasta carries gluten and is a refined-ish starch relative to whole-grain berries. Very large portions, eaten daily without legumes or vegetables, push the same refined-carb pattern any other white flour would.

foods.benefits_en: Wheat flour is a spectrum, not a single ingredient. **Whole-wheat flour** keeps the bran (fibre, B vitamins, minerals) and the germ (vitamin E, healthy fats), which is where the nutritional payload lives. **00 / soft / refined flour** strips both, leaving mostly starch and gluten — fluffier crumb, longer shelf life, far less fibre and micronutrient density. Both reference patterns favour the whole form; Longo's tradition tolerates refined flour in pasta and pizza dough where structure demands it, and Blueprint sticks to whole grains.
foods.how_to_consume_en: For everyday baking — flatbreads, pancakes, rustic loaves — use whole-wheat or at least a 50/50 blend with white. Reserve 00 for dishes where its low protein and fine grind genuinely matter (fresh egg pasta, Neapolitan pizza). Whole-wheat flour goes rancid faster because of the germ's fats; store it in the fridge or freezer if you bake slowly. Hydrate whole-wheat doughs a touch more than white; the bran drinks water.
foods.when_to_consume_en: A daily-baking staple in the eating window. The refinement level matters more than the timing.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category. Diets built almost entirely on refined wheat — white bread, white pasta, pastries — track with lower fibre intake, lower B-vitamin and mineral density, and the flatter satiety curve that often goes with refined-carb-heavy patterns.
foods.excess_signs_en: Contains gluten — not safe for coeliacs and irritating for some with sensitivity. A diet dominated by refined wheat at the expense of vegetables, legumes, and whole grains is the recognisable Western pattern that the longevity literature pushes back against.

foods.benefits_en: Corn flour — the finely-ground whole kernel, including the bran and germ — is naturally gluten-free and carries a modest fibre payload alongside carotenoids (the yellow pigment), magnesium, and B vitamins. Stone-ground or **nixtamalised** corn flour (treated with alkaline lime, the masa harina tradition) liberates niacin that's otherwise bound and inaccessible, which is why corn-eating cultures historically nixtamalised. Neither Blueprint nor Longo singles corn out, but polenta sits inside Longo's northern-Italian tradition as a whole-grain rotation.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Coarser grinds make polenta (slow-cooked, 30–45 minutes, stirred); finer grinds make flatbreads, cornbread, and tortillas. Pair with beans and vegetables to round out the amino-acid profile — corn-and-beans is one of the world's most-tested complementary protein pairings. A drizzle of EVOO and a shaving of aged parmesan finishes a polenta plate without crossing into heavy dairy. Choose stone-ground whole corn flour over **degerminated** versions; the germ holds the fat-soluble vitamins.
foods.when_to_consume_en: A regular grain rotation, inside the eating window. Polenta works particularly well as a daytime carbohydrate base under stewed vegetables or legumes.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Diets historically over-reliant on **un-nixtamalised** corn (with little else) showed the classic niacin-deficiency pattern (pellagra); this is essentially absent in modern mixed diets. No corn-specific deficiency at culinary intake today.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake. Highly processed corn derivatives (high-fructose corn syrup, refined corn starch in ultra-processed foods) are a different conversation from whole corn flour.

foods.benefits_en: Corn starch is the pure starch fraction of the corn kernel — bran and germ removed — used as a thickener for sauces, custards, and gluten-free baking. Nutritionally it carries almost nothing beyond energy: no meaningful fibre, no vitamins, no minerals. Its value is functional, not nutritional. Neither Blueprint nor Longo treats it as a featured ingredient; it appears in trace amounts in a handful of Longo's dessert and sauce recipes as a thickener.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Slurry it in cold water before adding to hot liquid — added dry, it clumps. A teaspoon is usually enough to thicken a sauce for four; more turns it gluey. Corn starch loses thickening power when boiled too long or stirred too aggressively, so add at the end and ease off the heat. In gluten-free baking it lightens crumb when blended with rice flour and a binder.
foods.when_to_consume_en: No timing concern — it's a culinary trace ingredient, not a food in its own right.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake. As with any refined starch, it shouldn't displace whole-food carbohydrates in the everyday diet, but at the teaspoons-per-week level it's used as a thickener, the question doesn't really arise.

foods.benefits_en: Semolina is the coarsely-ground endosperm of **durum wheat**, the hard wheat that gives dried pasta its bite. Its higher protein content (mostly gluten) and denser starch matrix are exactly what slow the glycemic release in al-dente pasta. Compared to soft-wheat 00 flour, semolina carries slightly more protein and a touch more carotenoid (the yellow tint), though the bran and germ are still removed in standard semolina; **whole-grain durum** flour keeps them. Longo's tradition treats semolina pasta as a central longevity carbohydrate.
foods.how_to_consume_en: The two classic uses are pasta-making (semolina dough holds shape under extrusion better than soft-wheat dough) and as a coating or thickener — dusting a pizza peel, thickening a North-African couscous, or finishing a gnocchi alla romana. Coarser semolina (**semola rimacinata** is the finer twice-milled grind) takes more water to hydrate than soft flour; let the dough rest 30 minutes before working it.
foods.when_to_consume_en: In the eating window, as the carbohydrate base of a meal. Longo's pattern leans on it at lunch more than dinner.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category. Diets chronically low in any whole grain — semolina or otherwise — track with the lower-fibre pattern noted above.
foods.excess_signs_en: Contains gluten. Beyond that, no commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: Bread is the everyday vehicle for grain in both reference patterns, and the quality varies more than almost any other staple. **Whole-grain sourdough** retains bran, germ, and the fermentation-derived organic acids that lower the glycemic response and improve mineral bioavailability — the loaf the longevity literature actually points to. **White industrial sliced bread** is on the other end: refined flour, fast yeast, soft crumb, sharp glucose spike. Longo's tradition treats real bread (sourdough, whole-grain) as a daily food; Blueprint mostly skips bread, preferring intact whole grains.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Choose long-fermented whole-grain or rye loaves where possible; a 24–48h sourdough rise meaningfully changes how the loaf behaves metabolically. Pair with EVOO and tomato, with hummus, with a bean soup — bread as the scaffold for a vegetable-and-legume plate rather than the meal itself. Stale bread becomes breadcrumbs (a Mediterranean thrift staple), thickener for ribollita, or the basis for pappa al pomodoro.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Inside the eating window. Daytime carbohydrate sits more comfortably with circadian metabolism than late-evening bread.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category. Diets that strip carbohydrates entirely often run into energy and sleep issues over the long term.
foods.excess_signs_en: A diet heavy on white industrial bread is the recognisable refined-carb pattern: blood-sugar swings, lower satiety, lower fibre. Real fermented bread doesn't carry the same signature at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: Taralli are small ring-shaped crackers from Puglia made with flour, olive oil, white wine, and salt — sometimes with fennel seed or black pepper. They're a refined-flour snack, but the EVOO content and the boil-then-bake method give them a sturdier, less-processed character than industrial crackers. They appear in Longo's Mediterranean tradition as the everyday savoury snack alongside olives and a glass of wine.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Eat them as they come — with olives, with a tomato-and-EVOO salad, alongside a vegetable antipasto. They keep for weeks in an airtight tin. The fennel-seed version pairs particularly well with raw vegetables and hummus.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Snack scale, in the eating window. A small handful sits comfortably as an aperitivo accompaniment; they're not a meal in their own right.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category.
foods.excess_signs_en: Salt-forward and refined-flour-based — a daily large portion contributes to the salt and refined-carb load. Treat them as a snack rather than a staple.

foods.benefits_en: Coconut milk is the pressed liquid of mature coconut flesh, rich in saturated fat — primarily medium-chain triglycerides (MCTs) like lauric acid — and the small payload of manganese and copper the flesh carries. The MCT profile metabolises faster than long-chain saturated fats, which is part of why coconut keeps showing up in keto and metabolic-flexibility contexts. Neither Blueprint nor Longo treats coconut milk as a featured longevity fat — both lean on EVOO instead — but it appears across both corpuses as a culinary fat for curries, dals, and creamy soups.
foods.how_to_consume_en: **Full-fat canned coconut milk** is the cooking form; the watery cartoned drink labelled "coconut milk" is a different product (mostly water, see plant-based milk). Stir well before opening — the cream separates and floats. Use it to enrich soups (squash, lentil dal), curries, and rice dishes; the fat carries the spice. A small can usually feeds four; you don't need much for the texture.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Inside the eating window like any cooking fat. There's no fasting-window concern with fats.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category.
foods.excess_signs_en: Energy-dense and saturated-fat-heavy. Daily large portions push saturated-fat intake higher than either reference pattern targets — the MCT framing softens but doesn't erase that. Treat it as a flavour and texture tool, not a default cooking fat.

foods.benefits_en: "Plant milk" covers a wide range: soy, almond, oat, hemp, pea, coconut-drink. Soy milk is the closest match to cow's milk on protein (~7–8 g per cup) and carries the isoflavones of the soybean; oat milk is starchier and carbohydrate-dominant; almond and coconut drinks are mostly water with a trace of the nut. The category is a useful dairy substitute in coffee, oatmeal, and baking — and Blueprint uses unsweetened plant milks routinely, since Blueprint omits dairy. Longo's tradition allows some dairy but tolerates plant milks freely.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Choose **unsweetened** versions — the default supermarket plant milk is often sweetened with cane sugar or rice syrup. Read the label for added oils and emulsifiers; the cleaner products list the plant, water, and a pinch of salt. Soy and oat foam well for coffee; almond and rice tend to stay flat. Many plant milks are fortified with calcium, vitamin B12, and vitamin D — relevant for anyone on a plant-forward pattern.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Inside the eating window. No specific timing concern.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Plant milks themselves aren't a deficiency category. A plant-forward diet that swaps in unfortified almond or rice milk for dairy without compensating elsewhere can leave the B12 and calcium picture thin — fortified versions or other sources of those nutrients (nutritional yeast, leafy greens) cover the gap.
foods.excess_signs_en: Sweetened plant milks contribute meaningful added sugar at daily volumes. Beyond that, no commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake of the unsweetened forms.

foods.benefits_en: A simmered extract of onion, carrot, celery, herbs, and whatever vegetable trim the kitchen has on hand. Nutritionally light — most of the vitamin payload of the vegetables leaches into the water along with the flavour, but the calorie and macro density stays low. The real value is functional: a flavour base that lets you cook grains, legumes, and soups without leaning on salt or fat to carry taste. Longo's recipes use vegetable broth liberally; Blueprint uses it where a savoury liquid is needed.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Homemade is best — simmer (don't boil) trim and aromatics for 45–90 minutes, strain, and refrigerate or freeze. A parmesan rind, a bay leaf, and a clove of garlic round it out. Store-bought is fine; check the salt level (the low-sodium versions give you control over the seasoning of whatever you're cooking). Use as the cooking liquid for rice, farro, lentils, and risotto; deglaze pans with it; build soups on top.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Inside the eating window. A warm cup of broth can also sit comfortably during the fasting window for some interpretations — it's nearly calorie-free — but a strict 12h water-only fast would exclude it.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category.
foods.excess_signs_en: Salt level is the only practical concern; commercial broths range from gentle to very salty. Beyond that, no commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: Eggs are one of the most complete single-food protein sources — all essential amino acids, plus choline (concentrated in the yolk and relevant for brain and liver metabolism), lutein and zeaxanthin (eye carotenoids), vitamin B12, vitamin D, and selenium. The yolk carries the bulk of the micronutrients and the cholesterol; the white is almost pure protein. **Blueprint explicitly excludes eggs** — Bryan Johnson's protocol skips them on a methionine-restriction and cholesterol argument. **Longo's Mediterranean variant allows a few eggs a week**, treating them as a moderate-frequency protein source. Both lenses are defensible; the choice is yours.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Soft-boiled, poached, or gently scrambled preserves the most heat-sensitive nutrients in the yolk; hard-boiled is fine but oxidises some yolk fats. Pair with vegetables, whole grains, and a fat (olive oil) rather than with bacon and white toast — the company eggs keep matters as much as the egg itself. Choose pasture-raised or omega-3-enriched eggs where available; the fatty-acid and carotenoid profile is meaningfully different.
foods.when_to_consume_en: If you follow Longo's allowance, 2–4 a week is the tradition's rough range — typically at breakfast or lunch inside the eating window. If you follow Blueprint, none.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Eggs aren't an essential food, so "egg deficiency" doesn't exist as such. Diets chronically low in choline-rich foods (eggs, soy, certain organ meats) can show the choline gap in cohort data; plant-forward eaters typically cover it through soy and cruciferous vegetables.
foods.excess_signs_en: Cohort data on eggs and cardiovascular outcomes is mixed and contested — the older "eggs spike cholesterol" framing has softened, but the signal isn't zero either. Daily 3–4 eggs over years sits outside both reference patterns; a few a week is where the Mediterranean tradition lands.

foods.benefits_en: Aged hard cheeses like Parmigiano-Reggiano and Grana Padano are nutrient-dense in protein and calcium per gram, fermented long enough (12–36 months) that the lactose is essentially gone, and carry the umami-glutamate profile that makes them a finishing flavour rather than a bulk ingredient. **Longo's tradition treats aged cheese as a small finishing condiment** — a tablespoon shaved over pasta or soup — not as a protein source. **Blueprint omits dairy entirely**, including parmesan. Both lenses sit on the same fact: parmesan delivers flavour density that lets you use very little.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Grate or shave fresh from a wedge; pre-grated bagged parmesan is usually a different product (often blended with cellulose). A teaspoon to a tablespoon finishes a bowl of pasta, soup, or risotto. The rind goes into bean soups and broths to add savoury depth — a Mediterranean thrift move worth keeping. Don't cook parmesan into a sauce over high heat; it clumps and turns grainy.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Inside the eating window, as a finishing flavour rather than a daily-volume food. If you follow Longo, small daily amounts fit; if you follow Blueprint, skip.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category. Diets that omit dairy entirely (Blueprint's lens) need to source calcium and B12 elsewhere — fortified plant milks, leafy greens, sardines, nutritional yeast all cover the gap.
foods.excess_signs_en: Salt-forward and saturated-fat-dense. Daily large portions (50 g+) push both the salt and the saturated-fat load; the Mediterranean tradition uses it by the teaspoon for a reason.

foods.benefits_en: Ricotta salata is ricotta that's been salted, pressed, and aged — a firm, mild, sliceable cheese from southern Italy, more delicate than feta and less assertive than aged pecorino. The aging concentrates protein and salt; calcium follows. Like all aged cheese in **Longo's tradition, it's a flavour finish, not a protein source** — shaved over pasta with eggplant (pasta alla Norma), crumbled onto salads, layered into baked vegetable dishes. **Blueprint omits dairy entirely.**
foods.how_to_consume_en: Slice or crumble directly onto the finished dish; cooking it dulls the texture that makes it useful. Pairs particularly well with tomato, eggplant, and basil — the southern-Italian flavour triangle. A tablespoon or two finishes a plate; more turns the dish into a cheese plate. Store wrapped in parchment in the fridge.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Inside the eating window. A small Mediterranean amount across the week, if dairy is in your pattern.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category. Same calcium / B12 caveat as parmesan for dairy-free patterns.
foods.excess_signs_en: Salt-forward — the **salata** is literally "salted". Daily large portions contribute to the salt load. Beyond that, no commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: Almonds carry monounsaturated fat (similar profile to olive oil), the highest vitamin E density of any common nut, magnesium, and a fibre payload that keeps the glycemic response gentle. Cohort data tie regular almond intake to favourable lipid markers and steadier post-meal glucose. **Blueprint** features almonds and almond flour across the daily protocol; **Longo's tradition** treats them as one of the Mediterranean default snacks. The skin holds most of the polyphenols, so leave it on when you can.
foods.how_to_consume_en: A small handful (~25–30 g, roughly 20–25 nuts) is the everyday portion. Raw or dry-roasted; skip the heavily salted and oil-roasted versions where the oil is usually a refined seed oil. Soaking overnight softens the texture and is the traditional move in Mediterranean and Ayurvedic kitchens; it doesn't meaningfully change the nutritional profile but makes them easier on the gut for some people. Almond butter and almond flour extend the same payload to baking and spreads.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily, inside the eating window. Either as a snack or worked into meals (over salads, into oatmeal, in baked goods).
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category. Diets chronically low in nuts broadly track in cohort data with worse cardiovascular markers — a low-nut pattern is one of the more reliable signals in the longevity literature.
foods.excess_signs_en: Energy-dense — a large daily handful (>60–80 g) adds up. Almonds also carry oxalates; people prone to calcium-oxalate kidney stones may want to keep the daily portion moderate.

foods.benefits_en: Hazelnuts sit in the same Mediterranean-nut family as almonds — high in monounsaturated fat, generous in vitamin E and manganese, with a polyphenol profile concentrated in the skin. They're a defining ingredient of northern-Italian cuisine (Piedmont in particular) and appear across Longo's tradition in pestos, sauces, and desserts. Blueprint doesn't single hazelnuts out but treats them inside the daily nut rotation.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Toast briefly (8–10 minutes at 160 °C) to develop the flavour, then rub off the papery skins in a clean tea towel if a dish calls for it — though the skin holds most of the polyphenols, so leave it on for everyday eating. Use whole in salads and baked goods, ground into nut butters, or worked into a pesto with parsley and EVOO. Pair with dark chocolate (the Piedmontese **gianduja** tradition) for a longevity-friendly dessert.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily, inside the eating window, as part of a small mixed-nut handful. There's no specific best time of day.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category. Same low-nut-diet pattern noted for almonds applies here.
foods.excess_signs_en: Energy-dense like all nuts. No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: Walnuts are the standout plant-based source of **alpha-linolenic acid (ALA)**, the short-chain omega-3 fatty acid — alongside flax and chia, they're the trio the longevity literature points to for plant omega-3. They also carry the highest polyphenol load of any common nut and a mineral profile (magnesium, copper, manganese) that mirrors the broader nut family. **Blueprint** features walnuts in the daily nut mix; **Longo's tradition** uses them in pestos, sauces, and as a snack across Mediterranean tables.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Eat raw or lightly toasted; high-heat roasting damages the delicate ALA in the oil. A small daily handful (~25–30 g, 7–10 halves) is the cohort-study dose that keeps showing up in favourable cardiovascular signals. Pair with apple and a shaving of aged cheese for a classic plate, fold into oatmeal, or grind into a walnut-and-parsley pesto. Store in the fridge or freezer — the ALA fats go rancid faster than monounsaturated nut oils.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily, inside the eating window.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Diets chronically low in ALA omega-3s — walnut, flax, chia, hemp — track with the broader low-omega-3 pattern (drier skin, the inflammation-marker signal in cohort data). Walnuts, flax, and chia together are the practical plant route to closing that gap.
foods.excess_signs_en: Energy-dense. No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: Pine nuts are the seed of stone-pine cones, harvested by hand from Mediterranean and Asian species — which is most of why they're expensive. Nutritionally they sit in the monounsaturated-fat band of the nut family, with a notable magnesium and manganese payload and the pinolenic-acid signature (a fatty acid specific to pine seeds, associated in small studies with satiety signalling). **Longo's tradition** uses them in pesto, in stuffings, and across Italian sauces; Blueprint doesn't feature them specifically.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Toast briefly in a dry pan over low heat — they burn fast — until just golden. Use in pesto (the classic basil-pine-nut-parmesan-garlic-EVOO build), scattered over salads, in cookies, or with raisins in Sicilian sweet-and-sour vegetable dishes. Store in the fridge or freezer; the oils go rancid quickly. A small handful is plenty.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Inside the eating window, as part of meals more often than as a standalone snack — they're priced more like a flavour ingredient than a daily nut.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category on their own.
foods.excess_signs_en: **Pine-mouth** — a temporary metallic bitter aftertaste that can last days — is a known reaction to certain pine-nut species, particularly some Chinese imports. It's harmless and resolves on its own. Beyond that, no commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: Pistachios carry the same monounsaturated-fat backbone as the rest of the Mediterranean-nut family, with one of the higher protein densities among nuts and a meaningful payload of lutein and zeaxanthin (the same eye-carotenoids found in egg yolks). They also bring B6, copper, and a generous fibre fraction. **Blueprint** uses pistachios in the daily nut rotation; **Longo's tradition** treats them as a Sicilian and Mediterranean staple, in pestos, sauces, and desserts.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Buy them in the shell when you can — shelling slows the eating pace and tends to land you on the right portion (a small handful, ~25–30 g of shelled weight). Choose unsalted or lightly salted; the heavily salted bar-snack versions push the daily salt load fast. Use ground in Sicilian pesto with EVOO and parmesan, scattered over salads and yoghurt, or in baked goods.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily, inside the eating window. A handful as a mid-afternoon snack fits the Mediterranean rhythm.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category. The broader low-nut-diet pattern noted under almonds applies here.
foods.excess_signs_en: Energy-dense. Heavily salted versions contribute meaningfully to the salt load at daily large portions. No other commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: Chia seeds are one of the densest plant sources of **alpha-linolenic acid (ALA) omega-3**, alongside flax and walnut. They carry a remarkable soluble-fibre payload — the mucilage that swells in water and forms the chia-pudding gel — along with calcium, magnesium, and complete plant protein. The soluble fibre slows gastric emptying and the glucose curve of the meal it's eaten with. **Blueprint** features chia in the daily protocol; **Longo's tradition** doesn't single chia out (it's a New-World food, outside the Mediterranean canon), but it fits the longevity pattern cleanly.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Whole chia is fine — unlike flax, the seed coat is thin enough that you absorb most of the payload without grinding. Soak 1–2 tablespoons in liquid (water, plant milk, yoghurt) for 10–15 minutes until it gels; eat as a pudding, stir into oatmeal, or use as an egg substitute in baking (1 tbsp chia + 3 tbsp water = 1 egg). Drink water with chia — the soluble fibre needs hydration to do its work.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily, inside the eating window. Many people eat it at breakfast for the slow-release glucose curve.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Diets chronically low in plant ALA omega-3s — chia, flax, walnut, hemp — track with the broader low-omega-3 pattern noted under walnut.
foods.excess_signs_en: Large dry portions without enough water can swell in the throat or gut and cause discomfort — always soak or eat with plenty of liquid. Beyond that, no commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: Flax is the third member of the plant ALA omega-3 trio (with walnut and chia), and the most concentrated of them by weight. It also carries **lignans** — phytoestrogens with their own cohort-data signal on hormonal cancers — and a heavy soluble-and-insoluble fibre mix that supports gut transit and steadier post-meal glucose. **Blueprint** features ground flax daily; **Longo's tradition** uses it less prominently but it fits the longevity pattern.
foods.how_to_consume_en: **Grind it.** Whole flax seeds pass through the gut intact and you absorb very little of the omega-3 or lignan payload. Buy whole, grind a week's worth at a time, and store the meal in an airtight container in the fridge or freezer — ground flax oxidises fast. A tablespoon a day is the cohort-study dose. Stir into oatmeal, yoghurt, smoothies, or baking; the gel it forms in water also works as an egg substitute (1 tbsp ground flax + 3 tbsp water = 1 egg).
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily, inside the eating window. No specific best time of day.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Diets chronically low in plant ALA omega-3s show the broader pattern noted under walnut and chia.
foods.excess_signs_en: Very large daily portions (>3–4 tbsp) can push the fibre load high enough to cause gut discomfort; introduce gradually if you're starting from a low-fibre baseline. The lignan dose at culinary intake is small and not a concern, though anyone on hormone-sensitive medication may want to flag it to a clinician.

foods.benefits_en: Hulled hemp hearts are one of the few plant foods that deliver complete protein (all essential amino acids) at a meaningful density — roughly 10 g of protein in 3 tablespoons — alongside a balanced omega-3 / omega-6 ratio (more omega-6 than walnut or flax, but in a ratio cohort data treats as favourable). They also bring magnesium, iron, and zinc. **Blueprint** uses hemp hearts in the daily protocol; **Longo's tradition** doesn't feature them historically, but they fit the longevity pattern.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Hulled hearts are ready to eat raw — no soaking, grinding, or toasting needed. A 2–3 tablespoon daily portion sprinkled over salads, oatmeal, yoghurt, or blended into smoothies covers the typical use. The flavour is mild and grassy, which is why they blend into other foods easily rather than standing alone. Store in the fridge; the fats oxidise faster than most seeds.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily, inside the eating window.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category on their own. Plant-forward diets that don't cover plant protein from beans, lentils, soy, and seeds together can show a thin protein picture; hemp helps close that gap.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake. Hemp hearts contain only trace cannabinoids — well below any psychoactive threshold — and don't show up in routine drug screening at normal food doses.

foods.benefits_en: The fat backbone of the Mediterranean pattern; ~73% monounsaturated (oleic acid), with polyphenols (oleocanthal, hydroxytyrosol) that drive most of olive oil's anti-inflammatory association in cohort studies. Longo treats EVOO as one of the two pillar fats of the longevity diet. Blueprint uses it in roughly half the savoury recipes for the same reason. Cold-pressed extra-virgin retains the polyphenols; refined "olive oil" has most of the fat but far less of the polyphenol payload.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Reach for **extra-virgin** by default and use it raw or with gentle heat — finishing soups, dressing salads, drizzling on cooked vegetables, light sautés. Smoke point is around 190–210 °C for EVOO, comfortable for everyday cooking. Store in a dark bottle away from heat; light and oxygen are the main enemies. A teaspoon of strong, peppery EVOO finished onto a finished dish is doing more work than the same volume cooked into a soffrito.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily. Both reference diets put 2–3 tablespoons / 30–45 ml across the day. There's no fasting-window concern — fats don't break a 12h time-restricted-eating window in any meaningful sense, but if you're following Longo's 12h pattern, the oil sits inside the eating window with the meal it accompanies.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Diets chronically low in monounsaturated fats — and especially diets that replace them with industrial seed oils high in linoleic acid — track in cohort data with higher cardiovascular risk markers and drier skin / hair. No "olive oil deficiency" exists in a clinical sense; the gap shows up as a missing fat *quality*, not a missing nutrient.
foods.excess_signs_en: Olive oil is energy-dense (~120 kcal / tablespoon). A diet that adds 6–8 tablespoons of oil to every meal without adjusting elsewhere can push past energy balance. Beyond that there is no commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: A neutral-tasting plant oil pressed from sunflower seeds, dominated by linoleic acid (omega-6) in conventional varieties, with high-oleic cultivars offering a more monounsaturated profile closer to olive oil. Vitamin E content is meaningful — sunflower oil is one of the richer dietary sources of alpha-tocopherol. Both Blueprint and Longo prefer EVOO as the default culinary fat; Longo permits sunflower oil for occasional delicate frying where olive oil's flavour would dominate. It is a fat with a different profile, not a problem fat.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Best reserved for situations where a neutral flavour matters — light pan-frying of fritters, batters, or fish — and for moderate-heat applications where olive oil's smoke point or taste isn't a fit. Look for high-oleic sunflower oil if available; it holds up better to heat and shifts the fatty-acid balance away from the omega-6-heavy standard pressing. Store in a dark cupboard; polyunsaturated oils oxidise faster than monounsaturated ones.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Occasional use, not daily backbone. The pattern in both reference diets is to keep sunflower oil as a secondary cooking fat, with EVOO carrying the daily intake. No fasting-window concern.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category on its own. Diets chronically low in vitamin E across all sources track with neuromuscular and skin-barrier complaints in cohort data, but sunflower oil is one of many possible vehicles for that nutrient.
foods.excess_signs_en: Diets chronically high in omega-6-dominant seed oils — when paired with low omega-3 intake — are associated in some cohort analyses with a less favourable inflammatory-marker profile. The fix is restoring omega-3 balance (fatty fish for Longo followers, flax / chia / walnut for Blueprint), not demonising the oil itself.

foods.benefits_en: A reduced grape-must vinegar from Modena, naturally sweet from concentrated grape sugars and rich in polyphenols inherited from the wine grapes. The dark colour signals the same polyphenol family that makes red wine and dark berries cardio-supportive in cohort data. Longo uses balsamic across his Italian dressings and finishing drizzles; Blueprint includes it more sparingly because the residual sugar bumps the glycemic profile of an otherwise low-sugar dressing.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Use raw, as a finishing acid on cooked vegetables, salads, or even strawberries. A teaspoon of aged balsamic on roasted brassicas does what a tablespoon of dressing tries to do. Cheaper "balsamic vinegar of Modena" is often standard wine vinegar with caramel colour and grape-must concentrate — read the label and prefer the unblended traditional aceto balsamico when budget allows. Don't boil it; the polyphenols and the aromatic notes degrade.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily, in small amounts. There's no fasting-window concern at typical drizzle quantities (1–2 teaspoons).
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category — vinegars are condiments, not essential nutrients.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake. The residual sugar in balsamic is meaningful only if a diet stacks several sweetened condiments together.

foods.benefits_en: Fermented red wine yields acetic acid alongside residual polyphenols from the grape skins — a sharper, drier vinegar than balsamic with essentially no residual sugar. Acetic acid itself is associated in small clinical studies with a modest blunting of post-meal glucose response when taken with carbohydrate-rich meals. Longo uses red wine vinegar in dressings across the Italian recipes; Blueprint reaches for it whenever a low-sugar acid is needed.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Standard dressing acid alongside EVOO at a roughly 1:3 vinegar-to-oil ratio. Works on bean salads, lentil dishes, and roasted vegetables where balsamic's sweetness would overpower the dish. Add at the end of cooking, not during — heat dulls the brightness.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily, in dressing-sized portions. No fasting-window concern.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake. People with reflux sometimes report that vinegar-heavy meals aggravate symptoms; that is an individual sensitivity rather than a population pattern.

foods.benefits_en: Lighter and cleaner than red wine vinegar, with the same acetic-acid backbone and slightly fewer residual polyphenols (white grape skins contribute less colour and less anthocyanin). Used across Longo's lighter Mediterranean recipes — fish preparations, lighter bean salads, vegetable pickling. Blueprint uses it interchangeably with red wine vinegar wherever a neutral acid is wanted.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Best for dishes where a darker vinegar would muddy the plate visually or flavour-wise — pale fish, white beans, cucumber salads, light vegetable pickles. Same 1:3 ratio with olive oil for dressings. Quick-pickling vegetables in diluted white wine vinegar (with salt, herbs, a touch of warmth) is a low-effort way to add a tangy element to weekday plates.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily, in condiment quantities. No fasting-window concern.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: A splash of dry wine — white for fish and lighter pasta sauces, red for tomato-based braises and stews — adds acidity, depth, and a small polyphenol contribution from the grapes. Most of the alcohol cooks off during simmering; what remains is the wine's aromatic and acid signature. Longo's Italian sauces use cooking wine as a deglazing agent across many of the savoury recipes; Blueprint uses it less frequently.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Use wine you would actually drink — "cooking wine" sold pre-salted in supermarkets is generally worse than a cheap drinking wine. Add it after the soffrito has softened, let it reduce until the harsh alcohol smell is gone (2–3 minutes of active simmer), then continue with the rest of the recipe. Skip the salt the wine bottle's label assumes you don't have access to.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Used in cooking, not consumed standalone. No fasting-window issue at the small per-serving residual.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category.
foods.excess_signs_en: People who avoid alcohol entirely — for medical, religious, or recovery reasons — should know that even simmered dishes retain a small residual ethanol fraction (typically 5–15% of the added alcohol depending on simmer time). Substitute with broth and a splash of vinegar if that matters to you.

foods.benefits_en: A small oily fish dense in long-chain omega-3 fatty acids (EPA and DHA), high-quality protein, and selenium, with calcium from the soft bones in the canned form. Because anchovies sit low on the food chain and live short lives, they accumulate far less mercury than larger predatory fish. Blueprint is plant-only and excludes anchovies entirely. Longo's Longevity Diet explicitly permits 2–3 servings of small fish per week and names anchovies among the preferred choices.
foods.how_to_consume_en: For Longo followers: salt-cured or oil-packed anchovies dissolve into the soffrito and add savoury depth without overt fishiness — a classic Mediterranean trick for elevating tomato sauces and braises. Rinse the salt-cured kind briefly before using. Two or three fillets per serving is plenty. For Blueprint followers: skip; the same umami can come from miso, tamari, or nutritional yeast.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Within Longo's pattern, 1–2 of the weekly small-fish servings. Inside the 12h eating window with the meal they accompany.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Diets chronically low in long-chain omega-3s — common in fully plant-based patterns without supplementation — track in cohort data with dry skin, brittle nails, and worse cardiovascular markers. Blueprint addresses this with algae-derived omega-3 supplementation; Longo addresses it directly through small fish.
foods.excess_signs_en: Anchovies are heavily salted; a diet chronically high in salt-cured fish stacks with other sodium sources and may push blood-pressure markers upward in salt-sensitive people.

foods.benefits_en: Another small, short-lived oily fish — sardines deliver one of the most favourable nutrient profiles in the entire seafood category: high EPA / DHA, complete protein, vitamin D, B12, selenium, and bioavailable calcium from the edible soft bones. Mercury accumulation is minimal because of their position low on the food chain. Blueprint excludes them as a plant-only protocol. Longo names sardines alongside anchovies as preferred small-fish choices, with a 2–3 servings-per-week allowance.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Fresh sardines grilled whole over high heat with lemon and olive oil are a Mediterranean staple. Canned sardines (in olive oil or water, not soybean oil) are one of the highest-nutrient-per-euro foods in any supermarket — eat them with the bones for the calcium. Pair with bitter greens, whole-grain bread, or a tomato salad. A squeeze of lemon helps with the iron absorption.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Within Longo's pattern, 1–2 of the weekly small-fish servings, inside the 12h eating window. There's no time-of-day rule beyond that.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Same pattern as anchovies — diets chronically low in long-chain omega-3s correlate with dry skin, hair, and worse lipid markers in cohort data. Sardines also provide vitamin D, which is harder to source from plant foods.
foods.excess_signs_en: Canned sardines are salted; in salt-sensitive people, frequent canned-fish meals can contribute to blood-pressure pressure. No commonly-reported excess pattern at 2–3 servings a week.

foods.benefits_en: A cephalopod whose muscle is notably high in protein and low in fat compared with finfish, with meaningful selenium, B12, copper, and iron. Cooked octopus is a Mediterranean coastal staple from Spain to Greece. Blueprint excludes it as a plant-only protocol. Longo's Longevity Diet permits seafood within its 2–3 servings-per-week guidance; octopus is acceptable though not specifically singled out the way sardines and anchovies are.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Octopus needs either long, gentle simmering (45–60 minutes) or quick high-heat charring after a tenderising step, depending on the cut and tradition. The classic Galician preparation — boiled and dressed with olive oil, paprika, and coarse salt — keeps the fat backbone Mediterranean. Avoid deep-frying batters that add a heavy refined-oil load.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Within Longo's pattern, as one of the weekly seafood servings if you enjoy it. No fasting-window concern beyond fitting inside the 12h eating window.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category — see the broader low-omega-3 pattern under sardines and anchovies.
foods.excess_signs_en: No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake. Octopus's purine content is moderate; people managing gout with their clinician sometimes track purine-heavy foods more carefully.

foods.benefits_en: Cephalopod muscle like octopus — high protein, low fat, with copper, selenium, B12, and a small dose of long-chain omega-3s. The cooking properties differ from finfish: squid and cuttlefish toughen if cooked between roughly 1 and 20 minutes, requiring either very quick high-heat cooking or long gentle braising. Blueprint excludes as plant-only. Longo's Longevity Diet permits within the 2–3 weekly seafood servings.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Either flash-grill or flash-sear rings and tentacles over very high heat for under two minutes, or braise whole bodies in a tomato-and-wine sauce for 30–45 minutes until tender. Stuffed cuttlefish with breadcrumbs, parsley, and garlic is a Mediterranean coastal classic. Squid ink is edible and adds umami and colour to pasta.
foods.when_to_consume_en: As one of the weekly seafood servings within Longo's pattern. Inside the 12h eating window.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category.
foods.excess_signs_en: Cephalopods carry moderate cholesterol; in older cohort studies this raised concerns, but current evidence does not link dietary cholesterol from whole-food seafood to cardiovascular outcomes the way refined-fat and refined-carbohydrate intakes do. No commonly-reported excess pattern at 1–2 servings a week.

foods.benefits_en: A lean white-fleshed finfish (red snapper most commonly) with high-quality protein, selenium, B12, and a modest amount of omega-3 — less than oily fish like sardines, but the protein density and the low-fat profile fit a longevity pattern well. Blueprint excludes as plant-only. Longo's Longevity Diet permits within the 2–3 weekly seafood servings; lean whitefish counts toward that allowance.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Bake whole with herbs and lemon, or fillet and pan-sear skin-side down in olive oil. Snapper takes well to Mediterranean preparations — tomato, capers, olives, white wine. Avoid overcooking; flesh should just flake. A whole baked fish on a sheet pan over vegetables is a low-effort weeknight option that lands inside Longo's framework.
foods.when_to_consume_en: As one of the weekly seafood servings within Longo's pattern, inside the 12h eating window.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category. The broader low-omega-3 pattern (see sardines) applies if seafood is absent and not substituted.
foods.excess_signs_en: Snapper is mid-tier on the food chain — mercury accumulation is moderate, lower than tuna or swordfish but higher than sardines or anchovies. Diets that lean heavily on large predatory fish over years can accumulate mercury; rotating among small oily fish and occasional whitefish is the standard mitigation.

foods.benefits_en: Stew mixes typically combine firm whitefish, mussels or clams, sometimes shrimp, and occasionally a piece of oily fish — the variety delivers complete protein, B12, selenium, iodine, and a moderate omega-3 contribution depending on the mix. Mediterranean fish stews (cacciucco, bouillabaisse, suquet) are a traditional pattern Longo's Longevity Diet accommodates. Blueprint excludes as plant-only.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Build a base of soffrito (olive oil, onion, garlic, tomato, herbs), add the firmer fish first, then mussels and shellfish that cook quickly, finishing with herbs and a squeeze of lemon. A slice of toasted whole-grain bread under the broth catches the saffron-and-olive-oil base. Buy whatever the local fishmonger has fresh that day rather than a frozen pre-mix; freshness matters more than the specific species.
foods.when_to_consume_en: As one of the weekly seafood servings within Longo's pattern. A stew counts as one serving even if it contains multiple species.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: See the broader low-omega-3 pattern under sardines.
foods.excess_signs_en: Stews lean on salty broth and shellfish, both of which carry sodium. No commonly-reported excess pattern at a serving or two a week; salt-sensitive people watch the broth volume.

foods.benefits_en: Whole cured olives carry the same monounsaturated-fat backbone as olive oil — oleic acid plus polyphenols (hydroxytyrosol, oleuropein) — with the added fibre of the whole fruit. The curing process (brine, dry-salt, lye, or oil) preserves much of the polyphenol load. Longo's Mediterranean pattern features olives as a regular snack and pasta-sauce ingredient; Blueprint includes them in some savoury recipes for the same fat and polyphenol payload.
foods.how_to_consume_en: As a snack alongside whole-grain bread, in puttanesca-style pasta sauces with capers and tomato, on salads, or chopped into tapenades. A handful (roughly 8–10 olives) per snack portion is a useful anchor. Prefer olives cured traditionally — water-or-brine-cured varieties retain more polyphenols than lye-treated commodity black olives. Don't discard the residual oil in the jar if it's good olive oil; use it in a dressing.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily is fine. No fasting-window concern; olives sit inside the eating window with the meal or snack they accompany.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category on its own.
foods.excess_signs_en: Olives are salted heavily during curing — a diet that stacks olives with anchovies, capers, and cured cheeses can push sodium intake high enough to matter for blood-pressure markers in salt-sensitive people. Rinse heavily-brined olives briefly if sodium is a concern.

foods.benefits_en: The brined flower bud of the caper bush carries quercetin and rutin — two flavonoids with antioxidant activity in laboratory and small clinical studies — plus the briny acid that lifts Mediterranean fish and pasta dishes. The bioactive contribution per serving is small because portions are small, but capers join the broader polyphenol-rich Mediterranean fingerprint. Longo uses them across the puttanesca-family sauces; Blueprint uses them more sparingly.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Rinse salt-packed capers before using to control the sodium; brine-packed capers are milder and can go straight in. Pair with olives, tomato, anchovies, and parsley for the classic Italian flavour profile. Add toward the end of cooking — long simmering dulls their bright tang.
foods.when_to_consume_en: As a condiment, daily is fine. No fasting-window concern at culinary doses.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category.
foods.excess_signs_en: Sodium is the main consideration. No commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: Cacao is one of the densest dietary sources of flavanols — particularly epicatechin, associated with improved endothelial function in clinical studies. The polyphenol load drops sharply as cacao percentage drops and as added sugar climbs. Blueprint uses cacao or dark chocolate (80%+) in dessert recipes precisely for this flavanol payload; Longo's Mediterranean pattern accommodates small daily portions of dark chocolate as the traditional Italian sweet finish.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Aim for chocolate that is at least 80% cacao — higher if your palate accepts it — and treat it as a savouring portion (15–25 g, two or three small squares). Bitter, unsweetened cacao nibs offer a similar flavanol profile and can be sprinkled on yogurt, oats, or smoothies. Dutched (alkalised) cocoa loses a meaningful fraction of its flavanols; non-alkalised cocoa is the higher-polyphenol form.
foods.when_to_consume_en: Daily, in small portions, inside the eating window. Some people find that chocolate close to bedtime disrupts sleep — the theobromine and small caffeine load are mild stimulants for sensitive individuals.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category.
foods.excess_signs_en: Most "dark chocolate" in supermarkets is 50–70% cacao with significant added sugar; a daily 100 g bar in that range carries the same metabolic load as any sweetened dessert. The flavanol benefit doesn't outrun a sugar excess.

foods.benefits_en: Mustard is a brassica condiment — ground mustard seed with vinegar, salt, and white wine in the Dijon style. It carries trace glucosinolates from the seed and adds piquancy without significant sugar (unlike most ketchups and barbecue sauces). Both Blueprint and Longo treat it as a flavour adjunct rather than a primary ingredient, useful for emulsifying vinaigrettes and lifting bean or fish dishes.
foods.how_to_consume_en: A teaspoon of Dijon in a vinaigrette helps the oil and vinegar emulsify and adds a savoury base note. Whisk into bean salads, brush onto roasted vegetables, fold into yogurt-based dips. Most supermarket Dijon is fine; check the label for added sugar (good Dijon needs none).
foods.when_to_consume_en: As a condiment, daily is fine. No fasting-window concern.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category.
foods.excess_signs_en: Sodium content is moderate; no commonly-reported excess pattern at culinary intake.

foods.benefits_en: A fermented-soy condiment that delivers concentrated umami through naturally-occurring glutamates, with traces of B vitamins from the fermentation. Tamari is the wheat-free variant of soy sauce (useful for gluten-sensitive cooks); shoyu contains wheat. Both Blueprint and Longo use small amounts as an umami booster, particularly in plant-based dishes where the savoury depth that meat or fish would otherwise provide is missing.
foods.how_to_consume_en: Use in small splashes — a teaspoon or two per dish is usually enough — in stir-fries, marinades, dressings, and finishing sauces. Pair with ginger, garlic, sesame, and rice vinegar for the East Asian flavour profile. Naturally-brewed tamari (long fermentation) carries more depth than hydrolysed soy sauce substitutes.
foods.when_to_consume_en: As a condiment, daily is fine. No fasting-window concern at culinary doses.
foods.deficiency_signs_en: Not a deficiency category.
foods.excess_signs_en: Tamari is concentrated sodium — a tablespoon delivers a meaningful fraction of a salt-conscious daily intake. Diets that lean heavily on soy-sauce-based dishes alongside other salted foods (cured fish, olives, capers) can stack high enough to matter for blood-pressure markers in salt-sensitive people.

foods.benefits_en: A traditional sweetener with trace polyphenols, small amounts of enzymes from the bee, and a flavour signature that varies by floral source. From a metabolic standpoint, honey is an added sugar — its fructose and glucose deliver the same glycemic and insulin response as table sugar at comparable doses. The micronutrient contribution is real but small relative to the sugar load. Both Blueprint and Longo minimise added sugars; honey is treated as the least-bad sweetener when one is needed, not as a health food.
